Those persons were interrogated and in order to get on with this, because of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shortage of food, or space, those persons were released. There was no court, after all, that we could pass the case on to. Statements were taken from them and this was postponed for sometime when conditions were in place to prosecute them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Bogilovic, was it both the civilian police and the military police that were carrying out these types of activities jointly whenever criminal acts were made known to you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably when I was authorised to monitor Mirza's activity. After the military police were finally separated from the civilian police, this would have fallen under the jurisdiction of the police, this would have fallen under the jurisdiction of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Bogilovic, you testified that you wrote a report to Mr. Avdic. Do you remember more or less what was the date on which you wrote that report?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say that this is the one document that I have not yet seen here. I would really appreciate having this document around, but please accept my apologies. The problems we faced at the time were so great that we didn't know what day of the week it was, let alone the date or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you also testified that there was a separation at one time between the civilian and the military police. Did Mr. Avdic inform you that Mirzet Halilovic would no longer be under your authority?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did. First of all, there were talks about Mr. Halilovic's work, and then it got out of control and I was responsible pursuant to a decision by the Presidency. I described his work and his behavior and said that I could no longer stand by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well as someone who was under your authority, did Mirzet Halilovic come to you and either resign or did you remove him from his duties?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no power to remove him from his duties because I had not been one to appoint him to begin with. He had been appointed as my subordinate and the appointment was signed by the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic. And the way I saw it, it should have been down to him to do it because he was the one I spoke to. He was the one who had ordered me to do that, so I went back to him to talk about that. I was his subordinate, after all. As for any other contacts, there was some tension, obviously, and it was very difficult to get to meet him. Contact was avoided. It was very difficult even to write this letter and live on once you've written it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did it come to your knowledge that Mirzet Halilovic was no longer the chief or the komandir of the military police?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any military meetings where you were informed that he would no longer be the komandir of the military police?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did and was told who might be the next in line for that job. Someone had to be found as soon as possible to take up duties and continue to work in that position, as prescribed by the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to return to P84. If could go to page 26, the ERN number would be 5077. Mr. Bogilovic, did you attend a meeting of the OS staff on the 22nd of November, 1992? Mr. Bogilovic, if I could direct your attention further down the page where you will see a date, 22 November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen the date. 22nd of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. There were meetings held on those days. Whether it was the 22nd or the 23rd, I really can't say. Probably so if that's what the record reflects. It must be true then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go to page 29 in the English version. It would be under ERN number 5079. And there is a line where it says Mirzet Halilovic's -- if I might continue to translate this part since it is only one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- if I may point this out, it is not -- at least on the English version that we have, it is not on 29 but on page 28. Seven lines from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think I am working on a slightly different formatted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, do you see where Mirza Halilovic's resignation, unanimously accepted. Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please point it out to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you see on that page the number VI? Can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a Roman numeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, let's not waste time. Can you bring it over here, please. I'm asking him to see number VI. This is here and what he should look at is this line here. Over here. Start from there. You see Sakib, Atif. Keep on reading and tell me whether you come across this line: "Mr. Halilovic's resignation unanimously accepted." Can you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can find it, but can someone please read this out to me, the whole thing? Because I see that here it says: Sakib, Dudic, Mirza Halilovic, and it says "unanimously accepted."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is precisely that sentence. I need no more. Mr. Bogilovic, then did Mirza Halilovic hand his resignation to you?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Bogilovic, you've testified that there was another person, I believe, who then was in charge of the military police after you. Do you by any chance know of that person's name?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Mirzet Halilovic was replaced by Atif Krdzic, also known as Sakib, from the village of Osmace. He was formerly a policeman of the Srebrenica police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There you have it right in the middle of the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person who is there; and if so, will you tell the Trial Chamber the person's name.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person in the middle of the screen, the photograph that I can see here, is Atif Krdzic, from the village of Osmace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, for the record, Ms. Sellers, do I take it that this is from 517?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, the still that the -- still photo that the witness is being referred to is taken from P517 and it is clocked at 5 minutes, 33 seconds, point 4. And the witness has identified the person in the middle as being that of Krdzic Atif. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bogilovic, were you aware and did you participate in any activities such as reorganisation of the military police in November 1992, towards the latter part of November 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for reorganisation of the military police, I don't think I was involved. Ultimately the military police fell under the purview of the army, if I may call it that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to show now Exhibit P11, please, to Mr. Bogilovic. Mr. Bogilovic will see the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, would you please look at the document and briefly read through its content.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this decision indicates that there was better organisation and better control. Up to this point, the police had been in town. However, no checks were conducted outside the town itself. This is when there was a proposal which was eventually adopted for the military police, depending on their strength, to go out into the field in order to exercise control and carry out checks of what was being done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did any authority that you had over the military police then cease prior to this reorganisation as reflected in the document?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. There was a change, a different person was appointed, and obviously this was eventually resolved. There was always a problem in terms of seniority. We didn't know whether the Presidency came first or the staff. It was here that I finally found out that the army was subordinated to the army and independent of the Srebrenica Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person whose name appears at the bottom of that document, is that the person who you testified earlier about who was part of the army staff, Mr. Osman Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the signature says, chief of staff, Osman Osmanovic which he was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, yes, thank you, we can have that document removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have a correction to the transcript. "It was here that I finally found out that the army was subordinated to the army and independent of the Srebrenica Presidency." It doesn't make sense. Because the army was subordinated to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was subordinated to the army? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we would like to know is what you stated exactly: Who, according to you, you found out that was now subordinated to the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That precisely was the problem; whose decisions were to be implemented? The decisions made by the Presidency or those made by the staff of the armed forces or whatever they were called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You haven't answered my question. You said before "There was always a problem in terms of seniority. We didn't know whether the Presidency came first or the staff. It was here that I finally found out that - who, someone - was subordinated to the army and independent of the Srebrenica Presidency." Who was subordinated to the army and independent of the Srebrenica Presidency that you found out now in November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the civilian authorities were subordinated to the president, Mr. Avdic. And the secretariat and myself, the civilian police were all comprised by this. The commission for housing related affairs, bodies of the Municipal Assembly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. It's a very simple question that I have asked you and it has arisen because we think that there is a mistake in the transcript. Who did you say that you found out, in November, that was subordinated to the army and not to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police staff, it was subordinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The civilian police or the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police. The civilian police remained under the War Presidency, or rather, the president personally throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Sellers please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Bogilovic, could the military police then make decisions independent of any civilian authorities, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police could make some decisions, but only within the framework of their military authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness now P12, please. Mr. Bogilovic will see the original. I believe we have the copies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, would you please look over this document. Mr. Bogilovic, would you confirm that this document is a document that appears to be directed to or concerns Atif Krdzic, the person who we saw on the photo who you describe as commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I have never seen this document before. Everything it says is true. It is true that Atif Krdzic, as you see the name stated, and that is the individual I pointed out in that photograph. That most probably, after his appointment, things would have improved. And that is why he is hereby authorised to make decisions on who would be removed and who would stay. I had the same situation in the police. I had some people that I had removed and brought new people in, because those other people that I had removed were not good enough for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You can remove the document from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, as regards the cross-examination, as we approach the end of the examination-in-chief, could you update us on how much time you require? You may sit down. Please remain seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it will take at least six hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please try to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I will endeavour to finish today. Certainly we are nearing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't take any risk at this point in time of not finishing by Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did it come to your knowledge during the month of December, 1992, that members of the OS staff wanted to resign?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did learn about that and I was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn the reasons why they might have wanted to resign?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reasons were read out by one of those who tabled their resignations; however, they remained where they were, they continued to work. I went to Srebrenica. They still stayed on at their work posts. What happened and all the rest of it, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of these reasons include commanders not taking responsibilities that, from the OS staff's point of view, they should have taken in terms of crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. We can show him the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I know that you are trying to economise in time but I would suggest that you go --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If he is asked what the reasons were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, and I asked him did they also include these reasons. Might I please show him now at this point 255, Your Honour. I was trying to lay at least the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, but let's go straight to the issue and put a direct question. If there is a document he may be able to be in a position to confirm that document and that would speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you direct him straight away to the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the second paragraph under number 1, Mr. Bogilovic and, in particular, the sentence that begins with, "We are afraid of the troops." In the English translation, it is on page 1, and that's what it states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please find out number 2 for the witness, and all he needs to read is the few lines before that, maybe five six lines before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It would be in the second paragraph, after "Statement of Reasons," and the second part of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where he is pointing "placis" [B/C/S spoken], he starts reading from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, have you found the place?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the English version also be placed on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: At the same time, if the witness does need to see the whole document so he understands it in context, what the pargagraph is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will give him all the opportunity to read the document, but for the time being -- I mean, he is getting confused even in finding this sentence. Do you see "placis"? Yes, four lines above number 2. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It is in Sanctions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you read that, please, and Madam Sellers will be asking you a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably I can. I will try to explain. I will do my best. The reasons, what all this is about is that on the 14th of October, these individuals were appointed and assigned, the decision was signed by Mr. Avdic. Now, in view of what I said earlier on, the dilemma was who the superior was, who was subordinate to whom and who was superior to whom as far as the staff of the War Presidency are concerned. And here precisely it was finally asked that matters be clarified, that is to say what the armed forces were supposed to undertake. What their job was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Bogilovic, you would agree that that is among the reasons that this letter was prompted by those who wanted to resign? Yes or no, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's right, that that is what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we now go to paragraph 4 of that same letter. In the English version it is on ERN number that ends in 3063. Mr. Bogilovic, would you read, just to yourself, and answer whether you agree that what is stated in paragraph 4 is also -- was also true at that time and is among the reasons for the resignation letter.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether that was their personal reason, I don't know. I can't confirm that. But the truth is that they would come in, from the field and from other municipalities, groups would come in and they had weapons with them, and there was so many people there that it was difficult to enforce law and order because the greatest problem was accommodation, food, water and supplies of that kind. To provide all that for a lot of people in a short -- a small area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogilovic. I would now ask you to go to paragraph 6, the second paragraph on paragraph 6, and just confirm that that second paragraph, that starts with, "We will not accept the guilt," was that also among the reasons for the resignation letter?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is the signatories that are saying this, that they accepted that, that they accepted working in the staff and their intention was to help, of course; to take part, to participate in helping, giving assistance. And that time will tell and the people will tell whether they succeeded or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, do you accept that as the reasons for the resignation what was stated in that paragraph, second paragraph of number 6? Just simple yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, judging by their answer, they accept -- they think that the people will be able to state their views in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen, you are miles apart. He is reading the first part of paragraph 6 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- while you are asking him on the second part of paragraph 6. Mr. Bogilovic, please, would you read the second part of paragraph 6. I see that it's not his fault entirely, because the second part is on a different page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are distancing themselves here. They don't want to take the blame upon themselves. Now, what blame I really don't know what this is about, because they carried on working in the posts and positions they were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogilovic. Mr. Bogilovic, as a result of this resignation, was there a meeting that was called to discuss the resignation letter that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that one of the reasons was that it was precisely because of this, at least I think so -- actually, it was a little strange that Mr. Oric asked, or ordered -- I don't know whether he asked or ordered -- that a meeting, a joint meeting be held and then this is what followed. There was a joint meeting where this situation, this question was resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Mr. Oric, quite naturally, since he was there, these were his workers, his staff, this part, and of course he asked this problem to be solved and that law and order prevail.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to have this document removed from the witness and please show him P14.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, would you please look at P14. And is this the order request that you've just testified about, concerning the calling of a meeting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it. However, this is the first time that I see this piece of paper, just like all the others. And I never saw it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you referred to the first time, does that mean the first time when it was shown to you by the Office of the Prosecutor, not the first time here in court?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. This investigative process with Mr. Nasir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did you attend that meeting that was called as --

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go back to P84, please. Page 43, under ERN number 5100. That's the termination of the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, if you would look at the document that has the ERN number ending 5100, you will see a date, December 23rd, 1992. Joint session. Armed forces. War Presidency. And you will see the numbers 1 and 2. And underneath that number, there is a name "Naser," and it says "Naser opened the meeting. He read the decision about leaving the OS staff." Is that what you testified about in terms of Naser's participation at the beginning of the meeting that was called as a result of the resignation letter?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite certainly. Because he asked the president and it was quite normal, and his first sentence is precisely that, that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember whether he read out the letter that's a similar or the same letter in terms of the contents that we just looked at in the previous exhibit, the letter you just looked at from the OS staff?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a letter here. Whether he read it out, Hamed or who. I think Hamed read it out. But he didn't read it out to the end. Zulfo interrupted him from reading to the end. He said: We know the reason and there is no need for you to read it all out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that letter the subject of discussion at the meeting that day?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was the discussion. That was discussed and other matters were discussed too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you to go to page 44 in the English version. It would be ERN number 5101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we move on to another area, it says here, on page 5100, "Hamed read out the decision to step down from the staff." The English version contains something different, because it says, "Hamed read out the reason for stepping down Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from the staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I noticed that, Madam Vidovic, and thank you for pointing it out. As I take it from page 43, that I have and that we have, I suppose yours is exactly the same, you see there, about one-third down from the top of the page, you see 23rd December, 1992. Right above that there is, indeed, Hamed read the decision about leaving the OS staff. But then if you go down, after 23rd December, 1992, and the -- you read the joint session of the SOS and the RP and then agenda, and then number 1 and number 2, then the first sentence of the minutes reads: "Naser opened the meeting. He read the decision about leaving the OS staff." So what - I don't know what the correct position is, whether what we have on top of 23rd December refers to some other meeting, but I don't think so. I think it refers to the same meeting. But I am not in a position to say what happened that day, and I am not in a position to decide which is the correct version of the two. But I wanted to point this out for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear for the record, that, Mr. Bogilovic, if you could just confirm, that the decision of leaving was read out in the meeting that day.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was read out and Salihovic Hamed read it out. He didn't read it out to the end because Zulfo interrupted him and said don't read it to the end. No need.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Naser Oric present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask you to go to page 44 of the English version, ERN number 5101. There is a part on the document that has small dashes, approximately one, two, three, four, five, six, seven. I would just like you to go down to the fourth small dash. It looks like a list of items. Mr. Bogilovic, my question -- thank you -- is that there it is written, at least translated in the English: "Ensure premises for the prison on the premises of the CK." Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, what is the premises of the CK?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was proposed by Ramiz. Ramiz was a former employee, or rather, used to work in the staff. And I think the CK Red Cross, Crveni Krst, Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might you indulge me one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when parts of a document are being put to the witness for him to have a look at the document, we can see here that in this is a sentence contained in what a certain person was saying. So in future, parts of these -- this memo must be shown in context. Not just the sentence out of context but the whole context of the passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I respect what learned counsel is saying. In a bit of my effort to be as efficient as possible with this witness, but also as it is formulated in this document, it looks like there were just a series of points that were being raised and they don't seem necessarily to be attributed to people but points that appear to be raised at the meeting. I just want to draw his attention to that one being point being raised and ask him to comment on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact you both tried in your own way. The only thing is that there is nothing in the text here that indicates that these were continuation of what Hamdija is supposed to have been saying before that, and the witness -- I'm glad, actually, that the witness pointed out that it was Ramiz, according to him, that pointed these issues out. So let's proceed. I don't think there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you answered that you thought that the CK -- I'm sorry, the transcript has just gone up -- the CK is Red Cross. Now where would this Red Cross, to your knowledge, be located, if any place, in Srebrenica? This premises?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross and the premises of the sports equipment -- and Batujo Saluvic [phoen] worked there -- those premises were behind the municipal court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to have a photo put on the screen again. We've already seen this photo. I believe we have given it a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It's P516, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, would you look at this photo again. Are the premises of the Red Cross, do they appear in this photo?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I really can't see it on this photograph, the one I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please give --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can see it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness was shown photo bearing exhibit number P516.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I ask him to please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, would you look at the photo on the ELMO, to your left, and indicate with the pointer where the Red Cross premises were. And is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness indicates the darker part of the building which is at the right-hand side of the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Could I also indicate it is on the ground -- it appears to be on the ground level where he is indicating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And he is pointing to the ground floor. Yes. Any further questions on this photo?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much. We can remove the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Usher, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to ask you, do you remember attending a meeting of the War Presidency on the 29th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should first have to see the minutes, because I can't remember exactly. I can't remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would certainly like to lay a foundation of what was discussed at that meeting. I'm wondering, might I be able to go to P84 and show him the minutes, and ask him if he can confirm it or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. The ERN number that we'll be looking at would be on page 5102. That's page 45 in my English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, I'm particularly looking at the minutes of 29, December 1992. If you would look under number 1, the second paragraph it says: "Avdic." Then the English translation, it would say, "After an operation ends, people take vehicles as they please." My question is, was there a problem with taking vehicles or other items after operations that were discussed at the War Presidency meeting, the joint War Presidency and OS staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. A discussion was held and it was asked that authorised persons should confiscate all objects, including vehicles, which did not belong to the people who appropriated them at the time. And it was even ordered - I think I wrote out that order, because it came under my competence - to the automotive society to record which vehicles had been repaired so that we should know. Because in some cases the body was damaged and not the motor. In other cases, it was the motor that was damaged and not the body. So that they should keep records of all these vehicles, what was done to them, the number of the motor, the number of the chassis, the license plates, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bogilovic, I would like to now go to the second page, page 46, and there appears to be a part of those minutes under ERN number 5103 where your name is located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, there is a Becir, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But he has testified he is the only Becir at the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him confirm that that is the right conclusion to reach.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask if Madam Vidovic could read the part that begins with the name Becir, and then Dudic, the paragraph under it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Nobody knows who has which vehicle. Naser knows what is in Potocari. If other units had taken vehicles, other than Potocari, it would probably have been a different story. The staff should have precise information on which vehicles are in what unit. The vehicle that is now with Soson should be at the staff headquarters. It would be better if the staff used it to transport units as needed. "Dudic: What Becir said is true. I was not at the previous meeting. I have a privately-owned truck. My unit (Tokolja Ivcici) has no vehicle. They brought me a truck from Sase that was out of order. The looted vehicles should not have passed through Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, do you remember that exchange between yourself, the other members of the War Presidency and with Dudic, which has been read out that has been attributed to Dudic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that there was a discussion about this and this guided us to establish law and order and to register, make a record of all of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that assist in controlling the looted vehicles that might have come about after an operation?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can say that they were looted or not because mostly they were vehicles belonging to Muslim owners. Because prior to that they were all taken away, and now it had to be established which vehicle belonged to what owner. And the needs for the hospital for transporting the wounded and injured in the units. Because in this case, for example, Soson took a vehicle, so he can't decide about the vehicle himself. The vehicle should be taken away, confiscated from each individual and turned them over to the units, if they needed it, or the municipality, or rather, the original owner, the real owner of the vehicle in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to object because the witness did not say at any point that these vehicles had been looted in an operation of any kind and that they were gained through an operation. And then he explained it in fact, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, he did explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That's fine. But he had agreed with the prior things that were read out from the meeting that he had understood that and heard that. So if he answered the question in a way that was truthful, that's what the Prosecution intends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. We will not be using P84 now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Bogilovic, in March of 1993 were you asked to become or to succeed Hamed Salihovic in his post as chief of intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in March. In April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. In April 1993. Were you asked to succeed Hamed Salihovic in his post?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who asked you to succeed him?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following demilitarisation, in Srebrenica, the generally held view was that peace was now there and that the war was over. Naturally, certain individuals aspired to certain positions, certain jobs, and they expressed desires -- for example, a colleague of mine expressed the desire to replace me. I don't know what was behind this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, excuse me. Did you receive a request or an order to assume the position formerly held by Hamed Salihovic in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did receive it. I think it was on the 18th of April, 1993, specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who made the request or gave the order?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The request was given to me by Masic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a piece of paper indicating that request or order?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I did receive a piece of paper, saying that I was hereby appointed chief of the armed forces, or something along these lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the person whose name was written on the paper, indicating that the paper might have come from them?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was signed by Mr. Oric. I didn't even see Oric at the time. I was revolted, so I asked to see, first, the president of the municipality, my immediate superior, and after that I asked to see Mr. Oric and had a discussion with him about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you go see Mr. Oric in person?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to see him in a flat, but Oric did not reside in Srebrenica at the time. He lived with his father, over in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your conversation with Mr. Oric that day, was it clear to you that he was the one who was requesting or ordering you or appointing you to this position?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on our conversation, I was led to believe that he agreed with this. I'm not sure how it was decided back at the staff, but based on what he told me, when we actually met, he agreed with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the piece of paper you're referring to, is that one of the three pieces of paper that you testified about earlier where you had the opportunity to see the name and signature of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is one of the last ones, the third one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because of the name being on the piece of paper and the signature, is that why you went to see Naser Oric physically, in person?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really pay close attention, I just saw the signature there, Mr. Oric's signature. You had to take a roundabout route, and we didn't know exactly what would happen. There was a colleague of mine who had also been a police officer before the war, like myself, and some other friends, to the effect that he should succeed me because by now it was peacetime and he should have the position. Something along these lines. Of course, I did go eventually. But also due to my illness at the time, the problem was eventually resolved. I first went to see my direct superior, Mr. Avdic, and talked to him about this. After I had seen Mr. Avdic, I went to see Mr. Oric. I talked with him too. I told him what my situation was, that I was alone, no family. That I was supposed to go and seek treatment for my leg, and that I would like to leave. I had to undergo a number of medical examinations with a Serb doctor in attendance. I was passed. I was allowed to board a helicopter, and that's how I eventually left on the 25th of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Bogilovic, then did you inform Mr. Oric that you would not be able to accept that appointment? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did inform him. We talked about that. We never even sat down. We just talked. It was perfectly normal situation. He was in a friend's flat, he came out, and we had a normal, decent conversation. I saw that he was having a difficult time, and so was I. There were no other friends for me to get in touch with at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bogilovic, since you were not going to take that appointment, do you know who was appointed to that position in your stead?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only found out later, but it was much later. I was already in Tuzla. Some time had passed and I learned that I was succeeded by Nedzad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say Nedzad. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what Nedzad's family name or last name is?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bektic, Nedzad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like the witness to see Exhibit P80, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, Mr. Bogilovic, if you could be directed to ERN number 30 -- 03055255, if the usher could assist us.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document I'm looking at, the one that I have in front of me, is not a document that I can comment on. It was written on the 19th of September, 1993. I was far away by this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bogilovic, I would just like you to go to the part of the document on the page number -- in the English version it is 8. It ends in 2555. You will see in the bottom half of the page that there appears the name, Becir Bogilovic. I would just like to direct your attention to the sentence right above that. For the record, I just want to say on the B/C/S version the ERN number is 02075848.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Has the witness found the part that he is being referred to, or not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, do you see where your name is mentioned? Then I would like to ask you to look one sentence above that.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name is mentioned right here, the previous page that this gentleman has just taken away from me. My name is mentioned twice, firstly the page that you removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to this page that you are looking at now. That's the one that you are being referred to. Go on the previous line. You see "OD 16.4.1993 - 29.4.1993" and the rest. That's the part we are referring you to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I might read it into the record in English: "From 16 April, 1993 to 29 April, 1993, the chief of intelligence and security issues was Becir Bogilovic, and from 29 April, 1993 that position was taken by Nedzad Bektic." Mr. Bogilovic, one small question: Is the date of 16 April a correct date or not, from your memory?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember the date should be the 18th of April, 1993. And it was on the 25th of April, 1993 that I left for Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So other than the specific dates, does this accurately reflect that you were asked to be the chief of intelligence and security and then you were succeeded by Mr. Nedzad Bektic?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably so. That's what I was asked to do. I didn't accept. I went away to receive treatment, so someone else had to stand in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the document be taken from the witness, and I would like to inform the Trial Chamber at this point I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very good. Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Madam Vidovic, can you start straight away or do you require some time?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I can start right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you may remain seated, as we agreed. Mr. Bogilovic, you are now going to be cross-examined by Madam Vidovic, who is the lead counsel for Naser Oric. Yes, Madam Vidovic. We will stop at quarter to two, as per schedule.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must apologise to you before I begin. We speak in the same language, therefore I would like to ask you the following: Please make a pause after my questions so that my words may be interpreted. I will try to do the same. Also, whenever possible, whenever you agree with me, just answer briefly "yes" if you agree, or "no" if you disagree, because I do have quite a number of questions for you. Mr. Bogilovic, you confirmed that for almost 20 years you had worked as a police officer in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are familiar with the Srebrenica area or the hamlets and villages?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew the local population and were familiar with its ethnic make-up while you worked with the police?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were familiar with what was going on in the area several years prior to the war in the late 1980s, in 1991 and in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, wouldn't you, that the area adjacent to the Drina River known as Podravanja was very important for Serbia in the late 1980s?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The local Serb population in the Podravanja area was under a strong political influence from Serbia itself, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Especially after Milosevic's photographs had been all over the place, because every single building and every single room had Milosevic's photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you, please, Mr. Bogilovic, try to keep your answers as short as possible. Once we get to the documents I may ask you for further comment. Throughout those years - and I'm talking about 1991 and 1992 - propaganda literature sent from Belgrade was infiltrated to the towns in the Podravanja area containing ideas about Greater Serbia. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Podravanja area was flooded with slogans, such as: "This is Serbia," the four letters S carved in the shape of a cross, and messages such as "Muslims, you balijas, get out of here, you Turks."

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time, misinformation was spread by the state security service of Serbia about the threat to the Serbs living in Srebrenica and Bratunac; is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what they said on the news.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That question therefore, it's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An atmosphere of fear and tension was created and mistrust was spread amongst the people in Podravanja?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both sides expressed fear when they talked to people who were free.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Serbian media had an important role to play in all of this, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were adamant that Serbs could only survive in a single state, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time, throughout 1990, 1991 and 1992, it was obvious that the Serbs from Podravanja were preparing for war?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, Mr. Bogilovic, that in villages such as Redzici, Dubrave, in Fakovici, foundations were laid for pontoon bridges to bring weaponry across the Drina into Bosnia, and that was well ahead of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the war. Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the pontoon bridges but they used boats to transport things across the river and I caught the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will get to that. You worked as a chief with the police prior to your retirement. You had a certain amount of information on the activities of the political parties in the Srebrenica area. The SDS was the leading Serb party, arming, in fact, the local Serbian population at the time. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It relied on the JNA in this. Does your information confirm that?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have information that they transported weapons given to them by the army. We found a large cache of weapons in Srebrenica once we got in. Military weapons, automatic, semi-automatic rifles, and a variety of explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were weapons that came from the JNA, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. Bogilovic, that the local Serb population of the area of Skelani, Fakovici, Kravica, Bjelovac and other surrounding Serb villages met the war armed, uniformed, and equipped?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree and all -- even in 1991, Mr. Karadzic forbid MUP to enter Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogilovic. They even had machine-guns and deployed artillery before the beginning of the war, in this area, did they not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the elevations which responded to the shelling were taken over by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The police of Srebrenica, as well as the police in Bratunac, in the course of 1991 uncovered the weapons transports at night by boat from Serbia. You mentioned that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslims from Voljevica captured Kosta Neskovic from Bobrije and handed him over to the police while he was caught in the act of transporting weapons by boat from Serbia. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrested Kosta. Because his brother was a policeman too. He was in my group. And I handed him over to the competent authorities, to the inspectors who were in the Bratunac SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is true, then, that he was transporting weapons from Serbia to the area of Bobrije, where he lived?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because he asked me for the password at one o'clock at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he could be precise about this, the identity -- the identity of this person. Did I hear you well, did you say Kosta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know his name and surname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, his brother was Dragan Kostic, and he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So would this person be Kosta -- what would his name be? Do you know what his name and surname was? Do you know the family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neskovic is the surname. His name was Kosta and he had a brother Dragan Neskovic, who was a policeman in the Bratunac SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslim policemen could not survive in Serb environments in 1991, could they?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, quite normally since there were growing tensions, then they would leave, both sides would leave and transfer elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you agree with me when I say that the Serbs, the Serb population, and not the Muslims, blocked many roads in Podrinje already in the month of March, 1992? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that there were roadblocks and that a doctor - veterinarian, actually - was arrested at Zalazje. And others were controlling this area, allegedly for their own safety and security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that other roads to other communication lines in Podrinje, in March 1992, were also blocked off by the Serbs. The main roads, in fact.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they started the blockades. They set up the first blockades. That's natural, but the other blockade came when they entered, or rather -- in 1991 in the place call Kravica, when they shot at a vehicle, where there were four persons there, two killed, two seriously wounded. That's when tensions came to a head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogilovic. The Serbs also set up blockades at other strategically important points, such as the Podravanja mine, the Sase mine, and similar features. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Podravanja mine is concerned, there was also a problem as to who the mine belonged to. But they took all the machines, the dumpers and all the other vehicles so the workers had to leave. Finally, they -- and they didn't go to work any more. Whereas the mine actually belonged to the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the workers, the workers had to leave their jobs, their work, you mean the Muslim workers, do you not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you heard and came across information according to which there were Serb camps for the training of the local Serb inhabitants. Is that right? For military training, for the military training of the local Serb inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I had was that this was done regularly and many of them were at Han Pijesak whereas a lesser number, about 300 soldiers, were trained at Perucac in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also hear of the existence of a camp of that kind in Skelani and in Vranesevici?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, you said that on the 12th of April, 1992, you were in Skelani.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that you saw armed soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth of it. They were armed. They were on the bridge, between -- separating Serbia from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogilovic. You saw them wearing camouflage uniforms and well armed in Skelani on that particular bridge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Wearing camouflage and the olive-green type uniforms that the former JNA used to wear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those were local Serbs from Skelani, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't recognise any of them because I had to look in front of me and it was getting dark. I didn't want anybody to recognise me, so that I just passed by as quickly as possible, looking in front of me. I didn't stop to look around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Do you agree with me that on that particular day in Skelani there were many people in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw those particular people up on the bridge. When I passed across the bridge and entered Bosnia, two policemen stopped me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will come to that in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was going, I would come across people who were in uniform and armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, what you saw, those people that you saw in Skelani, up on the bridge there, you referred to them as an army, soldiers, right, and not a village watch?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was the army; soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, you saw Serb artillery positions, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery positions? Where the army was, where the soldiers were, they had weapons and it was directed across the bridge towards Bosnia. But I saw weapons, yes; rifles, not any other pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving from Skelani to the Dobrak Muslim village that you described to the investigators, did you happen to see any machine-gun nests?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the exit to the Kalinjanici village, and it borders on the Muslim village of Dobrak blow the mosque there, that's where there was a machine-gun positioned and it was targeted on the village of Dobrak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Dobrak is a Muslim village, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a Serb machine-gun nest; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslim village of Dobrak already on that day, the 12th of April, 1992, when you arrived, was already shelled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in the village, it hadn't been -- it wasn't -- there was no shelling but there were no people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the traces of shelling then?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard that -- before you left Skelani, or perhaps later on in talking to someone -- did you hear of Muslim houses in Skelani having been attacked?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that, the next day in the morning. Or rather on the 12th. Jovo Muhajlovic in Bajina Basta, when I happened to meet him - and we knew each other well - I asked him to give me a car for me to drive to Srebrenica in, and he said, "Don't be silly, it's wartime and I'm giving you a car."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he happen to mention that Muslim houses in Skelani had already been attacked?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All he mentioned was that the butchers had prepared to attack them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Afterwards, did you learn that the Mehic [phoen] family was attacked and their houses?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the next day in the morning, because Sejdo said that -- and he was a salesman, he said that Mesari was attacked that night and that the mother had brought in some weapons to the police station and they had escaped to the forest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Vidovic, because I need to understand this. I see here that he said, "All he mentioned was that the butchers attacked them."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter seeks clarification: Mesari, is it a place or people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew three brothers, the Mehic family. They were rich. They had a butcher's shop. And one of them was a teacher at the school. I think he was the headmaster, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But this makes it even more confounded. Because if it is the Mehic family that were butchers, we need to explain a little bit how in one line we have he mentioned that all -- that the butchers had prepared the attack, to attack them. And then it seems that the Mehic family was attacked in the houses. So I need an explanation. What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mihajlovic, Jovo Mihajlovic, told me that the butchers had prepared to attack them, whereas it was the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, all right. Okay. I understand now. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more clarification, Mr. Bogilovic. Mr. Mihajlovic was a Serb, right? And Mr. Mehic, the Mehics, were Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a meeting with Mr. Jokic and some other people, Mr. Jokic was a Serb. Now, was he armed with an automatic weapon when you came across him?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was the same Jokic of the 12th, I didn't see anybody on the 12th, I didn't meet anybody on the 12th. So which Jokic do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigators, you mentioned a meeting with a certain person by the name of Jokic. I'm not linking it to the 12th of April at all.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have a meeting with a policeman who used to be a policeman in Srebrenica, and then I carried on my way and he arrested me, and his name was Slavko. I don't know what his surname was. And on the other side of the road, somebody asked, Who's that? and he said, I don't know, and the man came up to us, the side we were at, and where I jumped in -- I jumped into a crevice and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people that you met, were they armed? And did they have automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the investigators and when you testified on Friday, you said that you were stopped and searched by people in Bratunac on the 17th of April, 1992. They also had camouflage uniforms and were armed, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on that day the units stormed -- what was the name? The Arkan's men, Dragan's men, I don't know. I was in Bratunac, looking for food for my chickens and I was stopped at the DNC and they searched me. And they searched me and my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who stopped you, the men who stopped and searched you in the Serbian village of Viogoro, they were also wearing uniforms and were armed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Four of them wore uniforms and were armed and they did carry out a search. I shouted at them. I said: What are you doing? Why are you doing that? It was very cold that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, very much Mr. Bogilovic. They were local Serbs, inhabitants of the Viogoro village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they knew me and I knew them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, you saw quite a few people in Serbian villages in the Srebrenica area around the 12th of April; is that right? And it is true, is it not, that the Serb population already then was armed, in uniform, and had their commands; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of April, Skelani separated into a municipality of their own. They separated from the Srebrenica municipality. The road leading towards Srebrenica, I was checked on two places and on the lake at Jezero there was the Serb army, Serb soldiers were in the school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So they had their positions, their lines, their checkpoints already then, already at that time?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of April, yes, they did, at Jezero. They had a barracks in the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, it is true, is it not, that from that day, the 12th of April 1992 onwards, there was ethnic cleansing of Muslim villages in Podrinje?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Especially, I think, on the 14th when they killed in the Jezero area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I really think the witness should be asked to see what he means by this term "ethnic cleansing." I do not see any of the questioning up until this time period has led to that. We talked about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, have you heard of something referred to as "ethnic cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for cleansing, both sides were fleeing. Serbs went to Serbia and Muslims went towards Tuzla, Sarajevo, and other places. So much for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bogilovic, did you hear that ethnic cleansing was carried out of the Muslim population in April and May in the Podrinje area?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's true. It's absolutely true. There were mass arrests, mass killings in Voljevica, Suha and Glogovo, and these places were burned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that. We are speaking about now. It's only a continuation of what started occurring in Zvornik and Bijeljina earlier, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early May 1992, persecutions started of Muslims from the entire Skelani area, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they were sent off to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that on the 7th of May alone, in one place in Skelani, 17 persons were shot?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the exact figure, but, yes, people were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, 1992, many Muslim villages were burned, or parts of villages that were inhabited by Muslims around Skelani. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm this. I know there was -- there was an operation around Skelani, Dayegosta, and in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that many thousands of people were expelled and these people continued to live in the nearby woods; is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the war, Milici was a Serb stronghold; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to and during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People were also expelled in the Muslim villages facing Milici and Vlasenica, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both sides of Milici, facing Vlasenica and facing the bauxite mine, the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In late April, May, and June 1992, the Serbs carried out ethnic cleansing in the Muslim villages of Djile, Nurici, Besici, Stedra [phoen], Biskovic [phoen], Jangici [phoen], Turici, Sabici [phoen], Gradina [phoen]. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am full well. And Djile at the end too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first village I mentioned, in actual fact. Mr. Bogilovic, it's true, isn't it, that on the 16th of May, 1992, in Zaklopaca alone a police unit of the Republika Srpska from Vlasenica and Milici and a unit of the army of the Republika Srpska committed an atrocious crime against the civilian population, killing at least sixty persons, many of them women and children.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The refugees who fled told us about this. They came to the woods and they told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zaklopaca is a village along the approach road to Milici, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's actually between Milici and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does your information confirm, or what you were told by the refugees, that the Vlasenica and Milici police units led by the former pre-war policeman Rade Bjelanovic had an important role to play in these events?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Rade Bjelanovic as chief. I know that he was an administrator first and then was appointed chief. Whether he was in fact in command is not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also true, isn't it, that Muslims were expelled from the area around Fakovici and Ratkovici, weren't they? The population was expelled and the Muslim villages of Abdulici, Zapolje, and Orlica were burned down, as well as the Muslim section of Tegari. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After these villages, Voljevica, Glogovo, and others, they started taking villages one by one in a succession in order to free the Serbian land, as they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do know then that a crime was committed in Glogovo, Hrance [phoen], Suha, Borkovcini [phoen], Haljevici [phoen], but many civilians were in fact killed in those locations?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what the survivors told us and those who managed to escape the firing squad, because some people were shot too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going too fast. [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going too fast, the both of you, and you are not allowing an interval as well, and that is making it difficult for everyone. I see that even the transcript is suffering, apart from the interpreters that really have to follow you at a speed. That's number 1. Secondly, I would suggest that you try to wind up at the earliest possibility, because I wouldn't like to go beyond the scheduled time because of everyone here, interpreters, technicians and everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I only have two or three brief questions before I finalise for the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned on Friday, sir, that Hamed Alic survived the firing squad when civilians were shot in Borkovac [phoen]; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also confirmed that the population of Voljevici, Zalazje, and Bilaca was expelled.

utterances.speaker: BECIR BOGILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this may be a convenient time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation, as usual, Madam Vidovic. We will stop here for today and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9 o'clock. I don't know which courtroom. I don't think it is this courtroom, no. If I remember well, it is not this courtroom, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might, I would just like to hand up video 517. I believe up until this time period it hadn't been handed up. I would like to let the Defence know it is available, and also for the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. We will resume tomorrow morning. I thank you, Mr. Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of March, 2005 at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
